3. 
The Source of the Standard of Review—Section 706 of the APA^ The 
ultimate holding in Loper Bright rests on the claim that Chevron deference 
conflicts with Section 706 of the APA. That claim, in turn, depends on 
assertions about the APA’s text and pre-APA interpretive methodology.
Consider, first, the APA’s text. The Loper Bright majority stressed the 
language in Section 706 directing that “[t]o the extent necessary to decision 
and when presented, the reviewing court shall decide all relevant questions of 
law, interpret constitutional and statutory provisions, and determine the 
meaning or applicability of the terms of an agency action.” The majority further 
noted that Section 706 requires courts to “hold unlawful and set aside” 
“conclusions” that are “not in accordance with law.” These provisions, 
according to the majority, reflect the “elemental proposition reflected by 
judicial practice dating back to Marbury, that courts decide legal questions by 
applying their own judgment.” And the majority contrasted these provisions 
with the deferential review required for agency policymaking and factfinding. 
See § 706(2)(A) (agency action to be set aside if “arbitrary, capricious, [or] an 
abuse of discretion”); § 706(2)(E) (agency factfinding in formal proceedings to 
be set aside if “unsupported by substantial evidence”). By contrast. Justice 
Kagan’s dissent claims that Section 706 is “generally indeterminate” on the 
question of deference to legal questions, neither prescribing a deferential, nor 
a de novo, standard of review. According to Justice Kagan, “Section 706 does 
not specify any standard of review for construing statutes.” And Justice 
Kagan’s dissent resists the imphcations from the deferential standards under 
substantial-evidence and arbitrary-and-capricious review, pointing out that 
Congress expUcitly refers to a de novo standard in Section 706(2)(F).
